full_judgment:
Sheikh Hassan Arif, J : This appeal, under section 48 of the Arbitration Act, 2001, is directed against judgment and order dated 3-10-2023 passed by the Court of District Judge, Dhaka in Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 226 of 2022 filed under section 42(1) of the said Act seeking to set-aside the Arbitral Award dated 7-6-2022 delivered by the Arbitration Tribunal arising out of agreement dated 2-12-2015 between the parties. 

 2.1 Facts, relevant for the disposal of the appeal, in short, are that the claimant (respondent in this appeal) and the respondent (appellant in this appeal) entered into an agreement for the sale/purchase of the property in Gulshan Residential Area, Dhaka, being House No.6, Road No. 78 (old-34/B), Gulshan Residential area owned by one Khaled Rahim. Accordingly, the agreement was signed on 2-12-2015 at a consideration value of Taka 45 crores along with a brand-new Toyota (Crown) Car. According to the terms of the said agreement, the claimant paid BDT 5 crores on different dates which the respondent admittedly received, but did not allegedly take any steps as per the said agreement to complete the formalities for final transfer of the said house. Upon queries, claimant came to know that the respondent even did not take any steps for seeking sale permission etc. from RAJUK as per the terms of the said agreement. When contacted, respondent said that he would refund the money. Several meetings were then held between the parties in presence of common friends and well-wishers wherein the respondent repeatedly took time to refund the said money. That, suddenly, the respondent filed Money Suit No. 17 of 2019 before the First Court of Joint District Judge, Dhaka against the claimant seeking compensation of Taka 10 crores, followed by an application seeking attachment of claimant's car show-room situated at Banani, Dhaka. Claimant then raised arbitration clause in the said agreement between them and, accordingly, served arbitration notice on 12th May 2019 upon the respondent and appointed one Barrister Md Joynul Abedin Bhiyan as his arbitrator with a request to appoint respondent's arbitrator. However, getting no response from respondent, the claimant filed application before the Dhaka District Judge, being Arbitration Misc. Case No. 344 of 2019, in view of the provisions under section 12(3)(Ka) of the said Act. Respondent then appeared. However, the Court concerned in the meantime, stayed further proceedings of the said money suit filed by the respondent on the ground of arbitration clause in the agreement in order to facilitate arbitration between the parties. Respondent then filed application seeking dismissal of the said miscellaneous case. Learned District Judge then heard the parties and, vide order dated 2-12-2020, appointed two arbitrators and directed the said arbitrators to appoint third arbitrator who would be the chairman of the tribunal and, accordingly, dispose of the arbitration Miscellaneous case. 

 2.2 the said order of the District Judge, respondent moved the High Court Division and obtained Rule in Civil Revision No. 2424 of 2022 and also obtained an order of stay in respect of the arbitration proceedings etc. The claimant then filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 195 of 2021 before Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh against the said stay order of the High Court Division and, thereupon, the Appellate Division dismissed the said Civil Petition. Claimant then contested the Rule before the High Court Division in the said Civil Revision. Thereupon, a Division Bench of the High Court Division (one of us was party to it), vide judgment dated 21-6-2021, discharged the Rule and directed the parties to facilitate expeditious disposal of the dispute by assisting the arbitrators and the umpire (chairman). Respondent then moved the Appellate Division vide Civil Miscellaneous Petition No. 297 of 2021 followed by Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.1976 of 2021. However, in the hearing before the Appellate Division, the parties desired to appoint their own arbitrators. Thereupon, the Appellate Division appointed Mr Justice Mohammad Abdur Rashid and Mr Justice Moyeenul Islam Chowdhury as arbitrators for the parties respectively with their consent and directed the Tribunal to dispose of the arbitration proceedings expeditiously. The arbitrators appointed by Appellate Tribunal then decided to appoint Mr Justice Abdul Wahhab Mia, a former Judge of the Appellate Division, as the third arbitrator/ chairman of the Tribunal. Accordingly, the Tribunal commenced the proceedings on 11-12-2021 and fixed the cost of the tribunal and remuneration of the arbitrators and chairman. 

 2.4 Being aggrieved by this award, the respondent filed Arbitration Misc. Case No. 296 of 2022 before the learned District Judge, Dhaka in view of the provisions under section 42(1) read with section 43 of the Arbitration Act 2001 seeking cancellation of the award putting forward various grounds and raising various observations against the award and the tribunal itself. The said Miscellaneous Case was contested by the claimant by filing written objection. Thereupon, the learned District Judge, after hearing the parties, rejected the said miscellaneous case vide impugned judgment and order dated 3-10-2023 mainly on the ground that the scope under section 42(1) read with section 43 of the Arbitration Act is very limited as defined by law and the award may be interfered only on grounds mentioned under section 43 which the respondent could not satisfy. Being aggrieved by this impugned judgment and order, the respondent has preferred this appeal under section 48 of the Arbitration Act. 

 (b) By referring to Clause (A) & (B) of sub-clause (K) of sub-section (1) of section 43 of the Arbitration Act, he submits that the respondent in the arbitration proceeding was unable to pay the cost of the arbitrators and repeatedly made representations in this regard, but the arbitration tribunal most arbitrarily rejected their representations and applications to reduce the cost, which resulted in the ouster of this respondent from the arbitration proceedings and, as such, he could not contest in the proceedings. Therefore, according to him, learned District Judge has committed illegality in ignoring this aspect of the case entirely. 

 (i) that the period of limitation will be three years in this case and the same may start for counting purpose only when, the respondent refused to pay the money to the Claimant. By referring to the various correspondences between the parties, which are admitted by the learned advocate for the respondent, he submits that the respondent never categorically said that he would not pay back the money. Rather, he repeatedly sought time from the Claimant. Even in the Civil Revision mentioned above filed by the respondent before the High Court Division, his basic ground was that the arbitration proceeding was premature on the ground that he did not refuse to pay the money. Therefore, according to him, the point of limitation in totally immaterial in this case. 

 (ii) Further referring to the very agreement dated 2-12-2015, he submits that as per the terms of agreement, the respondent was required to comply with various formalities including obtaining sale permission from RAJUK on behalf of the original owner of the plot/land in question, but, admittedly, did not or could not obtain such permission and comply with such formalities. Therefore, according to him, limitation period also could not start in order to apply the limitation act in the facts and circumstances of the present case, particularly when there was no cutting point in the correspondences between the parties. In this regard, he has referred to section 19 and Article 65 of the Limitation Act. 

 4.2 With this note in mind, let us examine the disputes between the parties, in so far as we are permitted under section 48 read with sections 42 and 43 of the Arbitration Act. Admittedly, an award in the arbitration proceeding concerned has been delivered and the respondent has filed a miscellaneous case before the Court of District Judge seeking cancellation of the said award on various grounds invoking the provisions under section 42(1) read with sections 43(1)(Ka)(Kha) of the Arbitration Act. The Legislature has clearly made out by provisions under section 43 that only the grounds mentioned therein may be the basis for interfering into the award passed by the Tribunal. Therefore, the said grounds may be reproduced below for our ready reference: — 

 4.3 It appears from the submissions of the learned advocate for the respondent (appellant in this appeal) that the first ground taken by them is the inability ovralzo of any party as provided by clauses (অ), (ই) under sub-clause M quoted above. According to Mr Asad, since the Tribunal arbitrarily refused the application for reduction of remuneration of the arbitrators, in particular the chairman, the respondent could not contest in the arbitration proceedings and, as such, could not place his case properly. Therefore, according to him, this inability of the respondent should be taken by this Court as reasonable reason for such inability as provided by Clause-(ই) quoted above. 

 4.5 Therefore, the issue of remuneration of the Chairman or other arbitrators or the cost of arbitration has been dissolved by the highest forum of our judiciary, which, under no circumstances, can be reopened by this Court. Therefore, on the point of inability of the respondent to contest in the arbitration proceeding, we do not find any lawful merit. Accordingly, the respondent has no legal case on the said point. 

 4.6 Now, the question of interest, as imposed by the Tribunal on the respondent by the award is to be looked into. According to Mr Asad, there is no stipulation in the agreement between the parties as regards interest to be paid by any party in case of breach of contract etc. Therefore, according to him, deposition of interest was beyond the scope of the agreement and, accordingly, that part of the award should have been interfered with by the learned District Judge in view of the provisions under Clause-(ঈ) of sub-clause (Ka) quoted above, as the same was beyond the scope of the subject matter of the arbitration. 

 4.7 To address this point, we have examined the award itself, in particular the part which dealt with the issue of interest, namely, paragraphs 43 and 44 of the award itself. It appears therefrom that the Tribunal has referred to the provisions under section 38(6) & (7) of the Arbitration Act and finally concluded that in view of such provisions, the award money shall carry interest at the rate of 2% per annum more than the bank rate from the date of award to the date of payment. We have re-examined the said provisions under section 38(6) & (7) and has found that the Legislature is very much clear about the obligation to pay interests at the rate fixed by the Legislature itself. This being so, we are of the view that this issue does not need any further examination or deliberation from this Court, particularly when the provision of law is very much clear. In this regard, we have also examined the decisions in A. Latif's Case and BADC case referred to above, as cited by the learned advocate Mr Asad. It appears that those cases were decided on the previous law, namely, Arbitration Act, 1940, wherein there was no such specific provision about obligation to pay interests. This being so, we are of the view that the said decisions have no manner of application in the present case when there are specific provisions in the Arbitration Act, 2001 as regards obligation to pay interests on the award money at the rate fixed by the Legislature itself. Therefore, on this point as well, we do not find any case in favour of the respondent (appellant in this appeal). 4.8 Now, the question of compensation is to be resolved. On this point as well, the case of the respondent is that deposition of compensation is also contrary to law of land falling under Clause-(ঈ) of sub-clause-(খ) of section 43 quoted above. Therefore, we have also examined the relevant parts of the award dealing with this issue, namely, issue No. F, as dealt by the Tribunal under paragraphs 39-42 of the award. It appears that the Tribunal took cognizance of fact that the claimant paid the money of Taka 5 (five) crores to the respondent by obtaining money from his loan account maintained with a financial institution and that the said loan account was being maintained for the purpose of purchasing cars/vehicles as he was engaged in such business. The case of the claimant before the Tribunal was that since he incurred interests of Taka 78,727,998 as interest on the said loan, the respondent became liable to pay the said interests, and this position of the claimant was supported by the statement of the said loan account. On the basis of this, the Tribunal accepted such claim in favour of the claimant and, accordingly, directed the respondent to reimburse the claimant by paying the said amount as compensation. To address this issue, we have examined the provisions under the Arbitration Act, wherein we have not found any particular provision as regards imposition of compensation. However, admittedly, the agreement in question executed by the parties was executed in Bangladesh and it was within the knowledge of the parties that the laws of Bangladesh would be applicable thereto. This being so, it has to be implied that they were aware of the fact that the provisions of the Contract Act, 1872 would be applicable to such contract and if any provision of the said Act provides for payment of any compensation to any extent, or level, they would be bound to pay such compensation in case of breach of such contract. Therefore, as suggested by the learned advocates, this Court is of the view that section 73 of the Contract Act, 1872 is applicable in the breach in question in this matter. Therefore, the relevant portion of the section 73 of the Contract Act may be quoted below for our ready reference. 

 4.10 Keeping this provision in mind, if we examine the very contract dated 2-12-2015, it appears that there is nothing mentioned therein that the claimant would pay Taka 5,00,00,000 (Five crores) upon taking the said money from his loan account already maintained with a financial institution for his car business. There is no previous correspondence between the parties on record which even remotely suggest that the respondent knew, at the time of the entering into the contract, that the claimant would pay the said money from his loan account. It is true that the fact of obtaining money from loan account has been mentioned by the claimant in the arbitration notice issued under section 12 of the Arbitration Act, but, admittedly, the said notice was issued long after execution of the contract. Therefore, the very test which has to be satisfied for seeking compensation for any loss or damage caused to a person, who suffered because of breach by the other party as provided by the section 73, has not been satisfied in this case in favour of the claimant. Evidently, parties did not have any knowledge at the time of entering .the contract that the claimant would pay the said money from loan account already maintained by him with the financial institution. 

 4.13 As regards the point of public policy, we have rather found case in favour of the claimant. Because, it is the respondent who has delayed the entire proceedings by taking recourse to litigations and legal proceedings one after another. Learned advocate for the claimant, in the course of hearing, has given a list of various cases having been filed by this respondent, which, according to him have been filed to frustrate the arbitration proceedings and/or not to comply with the terms of the agreement. He has even referred to an observation of the Appellate Division in this regard, wherein the Appellate Division has observed in its order dated 30-9-2021 that the tactics employed by the defendant in filing frivolous applications for dismissal of the miscellaneous case instead of allowing the matter to proceed to arbitration indicates an attempt to delay the disposal of the dispute between the parties. This type of activity defeats the purpose of the scheme of alternative dispute resolution which is meant to allow quick and less expensive disposal of disputes.
